newsitem.title: HONG KONG: S&P says has no plans to downgrade Thailand.
newsitem.headline: S&P says has no plans to downgrade Thailand.

text.p: Standard and Poor's Corp has no plans to downgrade the sovereign ratings of Thailand, said S&P's managing director in charge of sovereign ratings, David Beers.

"We think Thailand is quite robust given its strong financial position to ride out current pressures without the ratings of the kingdom being jeopardized," Beers told Reuters in a telephone interview on Friday.
S&P rates the Kingdom of Thailand's long-term debt at Single-A and its short-term debt at A-1.
Beers said S&P "won't be putting Thailand on review for downgrade."
S&P was responding to an announcement by rival rating agency Moody's Investors Service that it might cut the sovereign ratings of Thailand
Moody's said that its review was prompted by concerns regarding the soundness of Thailand's financial sector as well as by constraints on macroeconomic policy-making.
But Beers said S&P's view of Thailand's creditworthiness has not changed since the rating agency affirmed the kingdom's ratings last year.

"We affirmed the ratings because the sovereign debt ratings were quite robust owing to the fact that the short-term debt problem was in its entirety a banking and private sector problem, and the government itself on a net basis is a very strong credit because local currency and foreign exchange assets comfortably exceed its liabilities," Beers said.

Beers said that since first rating Thailand, S&P has "believed that the pressures the country is facing are not ones that in any way are likely to impair the fundamental credit standing of the kingdom and that continues to be our position."

Beers said that even if the government had to provide support, either directly or indirectly, to the troubled banking system, "we still think that the underlying fiscal position of the government would remain fairly strong, at least strong enough to be consistent with the present ratings".

S&P welcomes recent steps to cut spending "as an appropriate response by the government to the situation where the budget was threatening to go into modest deficit and also to send a signal that the government is supporting the tight stance of money policy that was defending the exchange rate", said Beers.

Beers said S&P recognises that speculative pressure against the baht is driving up short-term interest rates, which in turn is accentuating the slowdown in the economy and contributing to the asset quality problems the banks are experiencing.
